The Irrawaddy River, also spelled Ayeyarwady. Myanmar's most important river, flowing approximately twenty-one hundred seventy kilometers from its source in the Himalayan foothills south through the length of the country to the Andaman Sea. It is the economic and spiritual lifeline of Myanmar, supporting agriculture, transportation, and trade, and flows through the heart of Burmese Buddhist civilization.

The river flows southward from the mountains of northern Myanmar through central plains to a broad delta on the Andaman Sea. This Irrawaddy Delta is one of Southeast Asia's most fertile regions and a major rice-growing area that feeds much of Myanmar. Yangon, Myanmar's largest city and former capital, sits at the apex of the delta and was the center of colonial Burma. During the British colonial period, steamboats transported goods and administration deep into the interior, making the Irrawaddy a crucial trade route.

Mandalay, Myanmar's second-largest city, sits on the river at a culturally and historically significant location in upper Myanmar. The Irrawaddy dolphin, a rare freshwater cetacean, is found in the river and is now critically endangered. Buddhist pilgrims venerate temples and monasteries along the river, and the Irrawaddy is sacred in Burmese Buddhist tradition.
